title: How far must we count to find neighbours with no letter in common?
description: The names of neighbouring numbers are compared letter by letter, first with the pairs in the book and then with pairs that share no whole word. The comparison is carried on in the Indian and the international names, and the pairs checked are summed up honestly.
teaching_notes: One idea: compare the letters of two neighbouring number names, and report what the search shows without claiming more. Watch for students who say there is no such pair ever, when the search only covers the numbers checked.

source: The words 'zero' and 'one' share letters 'e' and 'o'. The words 'one' and 'two' share a letter 'o', and the words 'two' and 'three' also share a letter 't'. How far do you have to count to find two numbers, one after the other, which do not share an English letter in common?
video_script.why: The child can read and write number names, and now compares neighbouring names letter by letter.
video_script.substitution: Write the names of two neighbours side by side and mark the letters they share; look first for a shared whole word.
video_script.anchor: the names zero, one, two and three in a row, with the shared letters joined by lines
video_script.payoff_line: Every neighbouring pair shares at least one letter

final_answer.value: No such pair was found in the numbers checked
final_answer.spoken: no pair without a shared letter turns up in all the numbers we checked

maths_rules: zero and one share e and o; one and two share o; two and three share t
forty seven and forty eight share the whole word forty
nineteen (n, i, e, t) and twenty (t, w, e, n, y) share n, e, t; ninety nine and one hundred share n and e
nine hundred ninety nine and one thousand share letters such as n, e, t, h, u, d

every pair of neighbours up to 30,00,000 (3 million), in the Indian names and the international names, shares at least one letter; the search stops there, so it shows no pair, which is not a proof for every number
video_script.design: One idea: compare neighbouring names letter by letter. The four names stay in the anchor band; the working band builds the comparisons. The answer says what the search shows and no more. No hard clear.
open_questions: The book (and the worklist) say no such pair is found 'however far we count'. A search of every neighbouring pair up to thirty lakh, in the Indian and the international spelling, finds no pair without a shared letter, but that is not a proof for every number, so the answer says 'in the numbers checked'.
